stages.title: The universe and objects in space
stages.hook: When you look up at night, what can you see in the sky? Are all of them the same?
explain: Space is everything above our sky. It is very, very big. In space there are stars, planets and moons.
A star is a huge ball of hot, glowing gas. Our Sun is a star. Stars look like tiny dots because they are very far away.
A planet is a big round world that goes around a star. Earth is a planet. A moon is a smaller world that goes around a planet.

example.q: Which is a star: the Sun or the Earth?
steps: A star makes its own light and heat.
The Sun makes light and heat.
The Earth does not make its own light.

analogies.home: Think of a lamp in a room. The lamp makes light, like a star. A ball in the room only shines if the lamp lights it, like a planet.
analogies.nature: A firefly makes its own light, like a star. A pebble only looks bright if light falls on it.
analogies.city: A street light makes its own light. A road sign only shines when car lights hit it.

stages.mnemonic: Stars shine, planets go round, moons follow planets around.
terms: A giant ball of hot gas that makes light.
A big round world that goes around a star.
A world that goes around a planet.
The huge place where stars and planets are.

misc.wrong: Stars are small lights stuck on the sky.
misc.right: Stars are huge balls of gas. They look small because they are very far away.

stages.limits: This is a simple picture. There are also many other things in space, such as comets and galaxies.

trip.prompt: Look at the pictures. Can you find a star, a planet and a moon?

questions.q: What is the Sun?
questions.why: The Sun is a star. It makes its own light and heat.

questions.q: What is Earth?
questions.why: Earth is a planet that goes around the Sun.

questions.q: Why do stars look so tiny?
questions.why: Stars are huge, but they are so far away that they look like dots.

questions.q: What goes around a planet?
questions.why: A moon travels around a planet.

questions.q: Which one makes its own light?
questions.why: Stars make their own light. Planets and moons only shine because a star lights them.

questions.q: A child sees a bright dot that does not make its own light. It goes around the Sun. What could it be?
questions.why: Planets go around the Sun and only shine with the Sun's light.

questions.q: Put these in order from smallest to biggest.
questions.why: The Moon is smaller than Earth, and the Sun is far bigger than Earth.

questions.q: Match each word to what it is.
questions.why: The Sun is a star, Earth is a planet, and the Moon goes around Earth.

questions.q: The Sun is the star at the centre of our Solar System. How many stars are at its centre?
questions.why: There is just one star, the Sun, at the centre.

questions.q: Why can we see the Moon shine?
o: It is a small star up there
It has a lamp inside it
questions.why: The Moon does not make light. It bounces back light from the Sun.

panel.q: Both a star and a planet look like bright dots in the night. How are they really different?
o: A star makes its own light and a planet does not
A planet makes its own light and a star does not
panel.why: Stars make light by themselves. Planets only reflect light from a star.

panel.q: Why is the Sun much bigger and brighter to us than other stars?
o: It is much closer to us
It is made of fire only on Earth
panel.why: Other stars are as big as the Sun or bigger, but they are far, far away.

panel.q: How can you tell a moon from a star?
panel.model: A moon goes around a planet and only shines by bouncing light. A star makes its own light.
panel.why: Moons follow planets and shine with reflected light, but stars make their own light.

teach.topic: What a star, a planet and a moon are
teach.model: A star is a big hot ball that makes light, like the Sun. A planet is a world that goes around a star, like Earth. A moon is a smaller world that goes around a planet.

points.ask: What is a star?
What is a planet?
And what is a moon?

stages.title: Earth, the Sun and the Moon
stages.hook: The Sun is far away, but you can feel it on your skin. How?
explain: The Sun gives us light and warmth. Without the Sun, Earth would be dark and very cold.
Earth goes around the Sun. The Moon goes around Earth. They move all the time, but we do not feel it.
The Moon is Earth's neighbour. It does not make light. It shines because the Sun lights it up.

example.q: What gives the Moon its glow?
steps: The Moon cannot make light.
The Sun shines on the Moon.
The Moon bounces some light to our eyes.

analogies.home: A mirror does not make light. It bounces light from a lamp. The Moon is like that.
analogies.sport: Players run around a field. Earth runs around the Sun, and the Moon runs around Earth.
analogies.nature: Sunlight warms a stone in the day, just like it warms Earth.

stages.mnemonic: Sun in the middle, Earth goes round, Moon goes round Earth.
terms: The star that gives Earth light and heat.
The world that goes around Earth.
The path one thing takes around another.

misc.wrong: The Moon makes its own light.
misc.right: The Moon only bounces the light of the Sun.

stages.limits: Pictures often show Earth, Sun and Moon close together. In real life they are very far apart.

trip.prompt: Look at the Moon photos. What can you see on its face?

questions.q: What goes around the Sun?
questions.why: Earth goes around the Sun.

questions.q: What goes around Earth?
questions.why: The Moon goes around Earth.

questions.q: What does the Sun give us?
questions.why: The Sun gives light and heat.

questions.q: What would happen to Earth without the Sun?
o: It would be dark and cold
It would be hot and sunny
questions.why: We need the Sun's light and heat.

questions.q: Does the Moon make its own light?
o: No, it bounces the Sun's light
Yes, it shines like a lamp
questions.why: The Moon is a rocky world. It only reflects light.

questions.q: Put these in order, starting from the one in the middle of our Solar System and moving outwards to the one that goes around Earth.
questions.why: The Sun is in the middle. Earth goes around it, and the Moon goes around Earth.

questions.q: Match the thing to what it does.
questions.why: Each one has its own job in our sky.

questions.q: A boy stands in a dark room. A lamp lights a ball. Which is like the Moon?
questions.why: The ball does not make light. It is lit by the lamp, just like the Moon is lit by the Sun.

questions.q: Why do we feel warm in the sun if it is so far away?
o: Its heat and light travel to us
It is just next door to us
questions.why: The Sun's light and heat travel across space to Earth.

questions.q: A girl says, 'The Moon is a star.' What is true?
o: The Moon is not a star; it goes around Earth
She is right, the Moon is a star
The Moon is a planet around the Sun
questions.why: The Moon is a rocky world that goes around Earth. Stars make their own light.

panel.q: People used to think the Sun goes around Earth because it seems to move across the sky. Why does it seem to move?
panel.why: Earth spins, so the Sun seems to cross the sky.

panel.q: Why is the Moon bright at night even though it makes no light?
panel.model: The Sun shines on the Moon and the Moon bounces that light to us.
panel.why: The Moon is lit by the Sun and reflects light.

panel.q: Which is the best way to say how the three are linked?
o: The Moon orbits Earth and Earth orbits the Sun
The Sun orbits the Moon, which orbits Earth
panel.why: The Moon goes around Earth and Earth goes around the Sun.

teach.topic: How the Sun, Earth and Moon fit together
teach.model: The Sun is a star that gives light and heat. Earth goes around the Sun. The Moon goes around Earth and shines because the Sun lights it.

points.ask: What does the Sun do for us?
What does Earth do?
What about the Moon?

stages.title: Day and night
stages.hook: Why is it light when you wake up, and dark when you go to sleep?
explain: Earth spins like a top. One spin takes one day, which is 24 hours.
The side of Earth that faces the Sun has day. The side turned away from the Sun has night.
The Sun does not go away at night. Our side of Earth has just turned away from it.

example.q: It is night where you live. Is it night everywhere?
steps: Half of Earth faces the Sun.
The other half faces away.
So when it is night here, it is day on the other side.
example.a: No. It is day on the other side of Earth.

analogies.home: Spin a ball in front of a lamp. The side near the lamp is bright. The far side is dark.
analogies.city: When it is bedtime in one city, children in another city are eating lunch.
analogies.nature: Sunflowers turn to the light. Earth turns, so we meet the light and leave it.

stages.mnemonic: Earth spins, the Sun stays, we get day and night each day.
terms: The time when our side of Earth faces the Sun.
The time when our side faces away from the Sun.
One of the 24 parts of a day.

misc.wrong: The Sun moves around Earth and goes to sleep at night.
misc.right: Earth spins. Our side turns away from the Sun, so it is night.

stages.limits: Near the poles, the Sun can stay up or down for weeks at some times of year.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of Earth with one half in light and one half in dark.

questions.q: What makes day and night?
questions.why: Earth spins, so each side faces the Sun, then turns away.

questions.q: When our side of Earth faces the Sun, it is...
questions.why: Facing the Sun means daylight.

questions.q: When our side turns away from the Sun, it is...
questions.why: Turned away from the Sun means darkness.

questions.q: How many hours are in one day?
questions.why: Earth spins once in about 24 hours.

questions.q: Where is the Sun at night?
o: Still shining on the other side of Earth
questions.why: The Sun keeps shining. Our side just faces away.

questions.q: It is lunchtime in Kenya. What time of day might it be on the other side of the world?
questions.why: The far side of Earth faces away from the Sun, so it is night.

questions.q: Put the day in order.
questions.why: The day goes from morning to noon to evening to night.

questions.q: Match each to what we do.
questions.why: Daylight and dark follow each other because Earth spins.

questions.q: Pia spins a ball in front of a lamp. What does the ball show?
o: The Moon's path across the sky
questions.why: The lit side is like day and the dark side is like night.

questions.q: Why does the Sun seem to rise and set?
o: Because the Sun hops up and down
questions.why: We spin with Earth, so the Sun seems to move across the sky.

panel.q: If Earth did not spin, what would happen to one side?
o: It would stay in day while the other stays in night
It would be dark on both sides
Day and night would be the same
The Moon would vanish from the sky
panel.why: Spinning gives each side its turn. Without it, one side would keep facing the Sun.

panel.q: Why is it dark at night?
panel.model: Earth spins and our side turns away from the Sun.
panel.why: Night comes when our side faces away from the Sun.

panel.q: Why is it day in Japan when it is night in Brazil?
o: Earth is round, so only half faces the Sun
Japan is much bigger than Brazil
panel.why: Earth is a ball, so the Sun can only light half of it at a time.

teach.topic: Why we have day and night
teach.model: Earth is like a ball that spins. The side facing the Sun is bright, so it is day. The side turned away is dark, so it is night. One spin takes 24 hours.

points.ask: What does Earth do?
What does the Sun do for day?
How long does one spin take, and what happens on the dark side?

stages.title: Seasons and basic Earth movements
stages.hook: Why is it hot in some months and cold in others?
explain: Earth goes around the Sun once in a year. That takes about 365 days.
Earth is tilted, like a leaning top. As Earth goes around, different parts lean toward the Sun at different times.

When our part leans toward the Sun it is warmer, like summer. When it leans away it is colder, like winter. Near the middle of Earth the weather changes less, and some places have a wet and a dry season.

example.q: How many days make one year?
steps: Earth goes once around the Sun.
This takes about 365 days.

analogies.farm: Farmers plant when rain comes and harvest later. The seasons tell them when.
analogies.nature: Trees grow leaves in warm months. Some drop leaves when it gets cold.
analogies.home: Walk around a lamp while leaning. Sometimes your face is closer to the light and gets more of it.

stages.mnemonic: Earth leans and travels round, so each season comes around.
terms: The time Earth takes to go once around the Sun.
A part of the year with its own weather.

misc.wrong: It is summer when Earth is closest to the Sun.
misc.right: Seasons come from Earth's tilt, not from being closer or farther from the Sun.

stages.limits: Not all places have four seasons. Many warm places have a wet season and a dry season.

trip.prompt: Look at pictures of the same tree in four seasons.

questions.q: How long does Earth take to go around the Sun?
questions.why: One trip around the Sun is one year.

questions.q: About how many days are in one year? Round to the nearest day.
questions.why: A year is about 365 days.

questions.q: What makes the seasons?
o: Earth's tilt as it goes around the Sun
Clouds that cover the Sun in winter
questions.why: Earth leans, so the Sun's light hits different places differently through the year.

questions.q: Which season is usually coldest in a place with four seasons?
questions.why: Winter is the cold season.

questions.q: A place leans toward the Sun. Is it likely to be warmer or colder?
questions.why: Leaning toward the Sun gives more sunlight, so it gets warmer.

questions.q: Put the seasons in order, starting with spring.
questions.why: The seasons repeat in this order each year.

questions.q: Match the time to the movement.
pairs: Earth goes around the Sun once
questions.why: Spinning gives a day, going around the Sun gives a year, and the Moon's trip gives a month.

questions.q: A farmer in a warm land has a wet season and a dry season. Why might they not have snow?
o: The place stays warm all year
The Moon stops it from coming
questions.why: Places near the middle of Earth stay warm, so they have wet and dry seasons instead.

questions.q: Mia says summer is when Earth is closest to the Sun. Is she right?
o: Yes, it is true in winter only
questions.why: Seasons come from tilt, not from distance.

questions.q: If Earth were not tilted, what would change?
o: We would not have seasons like we do
There would be no day or night at all
questions.why: The tilt makes the seasons.

panel.q: It is summer in Australia. What is the season in Canada at that time?
panel.why: When the south leans toward the Sun, the north leans away, so seasons are opposite.

panel.q: Why do we have seasons?
panel.model: Earth is tilted and goes around the Sun, so parts lean toward or away from the Sun in different months.
panel.why: Tilt plus the yearly trip around the Sun give the seasons.

panel.q: Which movement of Earth makes a year?
o: Spinning once on its own axis
panel.why: A year is one orbit around the Sun.

teach.model: Earth goes around the Sun in a year and is tilted. When our part leans toward the Sun it gets more sunlight and is warm. When it leans away it is cold.

points.ask: What is special about how Earth sits?
How long is the trip around the Sun?
So how does that change the weather?

stages.title: Identifying planets and stars
stages.hook: Can you tell a planet from a star just by looking at the night sky?
explain: There are eight planets that go around our Sun. They are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Stars twinkle. That means they flicker a little. Planets shine with a steadier light.
A star pattern is a group of stars that people imagined as a picture. People in many lands made up stories about them.

example.q: A bright dot shines steadily and does not twinkle. Is it more likely a star or a planet?
steps: Stars twinkle.
Planets shine steadily.
This dot does not twinkle.

analogies.home: A candle flickers far away, like a star. A torch light close by stays steady, like a planet.
analogies.sea: Sailors used star patterns to find their way.
analogies.nature: Fireflies flicker. A steady lamp does not.

terms: A world that goes around the Sun.
A giant ball of hot gas.
A pattern of stars with a name.

misc.wrong: Everything bright in the night sky is a star.
misc.right: Some bright dots are planets. Planets shine steady and do not twinkle.

stages.limits: Twinkling is a helpful hint, not a perfect test.

trip.prompt: Find the eight planets. Which one is closest to the Sun?

questions.q: How many planets go around the Sun?
questions.why: There are eight planets.

questions.q: Which planet do we live on?
questions.why: We live on Earth.

questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.why: Mercury is the nearest planet to the Sun.

questions.q: A dot in the sky flickers and twinkles. What is it most likely to be?
questions.why: Stars twinkle. Planets look steadier.

questions.q: Which planet has big rings that we can see in a small telescope?
questions.why: Saturn is famous for its bright rings.

questions.q: The biggest planet is...
questions.why: Jupiter is the biggest planet.

questions.q: Put these planets in order from the Sun: Earth, Mercury, Mars.
questions.why: From the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars.

questions.q: Match the planet to a fact.
questions.why: Each planet has its own look.

questions.q: A bright dot shines steady. What might it be?
questions.why: Steady bright dots are often planets.

questions.q: Why were star patterns useful long ago?
o: People used them to find directions and seasons
They made rain fall on the crops
questions.why: People in many lands used star patterns to find their way and to know when the seasons changed.

panel.q: Why do planets not twinkle as much as stars?
o: They look like tiny discs, not points, so they flicker less
They are hotter than stars, so they glow steadily
They are closer than the Moon
panel.why: Planets are close enough to look like tiny discs, so air flicker averages out.

panel.q: How can you tell a planet from a star in the night sky?
panel.model: A planet shines with a steady light, while a star twinkles.
panel.why: Steady light usually means a planet, flicker means a star.

panel.q: The Sun is a star. Why does it not look like the other stars?
o: It is much closer to us
It is not a star at all
panel.why: The Sun is the nearest star, so it looks huge and bright.

teach.topic: How to tell a planet from a star
teach.model: A planet goes around the Sun and shines with a steady light. A star is a giant glowing ball that twinkles. There are eight planets, like Earth, Mars and Jupiter.

points.ask: What is a planet?
How does a star look?
How does a planet look, and can you name one?

stages.title: Movement, pushing and pulling
stages.hook: How can you make a ball start to roll, then stop?
explain: A push moves something away from you. A pull moves it closer to you. Pushes and pulls are called forces.
A big push makes something move fast. A small push makes it move slowly.
Things slow down and stop because of rubbing, called friction. A rough floor stops a ball sooner than a smooth floor.

example.q: You roll a ball on grass and on a smooth floor. On which does it roll farther?
steps: Grass is rough, so there is more rubbing.
A smooth floor has less rubbing.
Less rubbing means it rolls farther.

analogies.home: You push a door to open it and pull a drawer to open it.
analogies.sport: You kick a ball to push it. A goalkeeper dives to stop it.
analogies.farm: A farmer pulls a cart, and pushes a wheelbarrow.

stages.mnemonic: Push away, pull near, rub slows you here.
terms: A force that moves something away.
A force that moves something closer.

misc.right: Things stop because a force, like rubbing, stops them.

stages.limits: In space there is almost no rubbing, so things keep moving for a very long time.

trip.prompt: Look for pictures of pushes and pulls.

questions.q: What do you do to open a drawer?
questions.why: You pull a drawer toward you.

questions.q: What do you do to move a swing away from you?
questions.why: A push moves it away.

questions.q: A push or a pull is called a...
questions.why: Pushes and pulls are forces.

questions.q: A bigger push makes a ball go...
questions.why: A bigger force gives more speed.

questions.q: Which stops a toy car sooner?
questions.why: Rough surfaces have more friction.

questions.q: Match each action to push or pull.
questions.why: A push moves away, a pull moves toward you.

questions.q: Put these in order from least rubbing to most rubbing.
questions.why: Ice is slippery, sand and grass are rough and slow things quickly.

questions.q: Tomas wants his sled to slide far. Where should he sled?
questions.why: Smooth snow has little friction.

questions.q: Why do we put rough soles on boots?
o: They grip the ground and stop slipping
They make us fly high up
questions.why: Rough soles have more friction, so feet do not slip.

questions.q: Why does a ball in space keep rolling for a long time?
o: There is almost nothing to rub against
Space has a strong wind that keeps pushing it on
questions.why: Without rubbing or other forces, motion does not slow down.

panel.q: You pull a wagon and it starts to move. What changed?
panel.why: A pull is a force that starts motion.

panel.q: Why does a ball stop rolling on the floor?
panel.model: The rubbing between the ball and the floor, called friction, slows it down until it stops.
panel.why: Friction is a force that slows moving things.

panel.q: Which has more friction?
panel.why: Sandpaper is rough, so it has a lot of friction.

teach.model: A push moves things away and a pull brings them closer. They are called forces. A bigger force makes things move faster. Friction is rubbing that slows things down, like a ball on rough grass.

points.ask: What are a push and a pull?
What do we call them together?
Why do things stop moving?

stages.title: Light, shadows and colours
stages.hook: Why does your shadow get long in the evening and short at noon?
explain: Light comes from things like the Sun, lamps and fires. Light travels in straight lines.
A shadow is made when something blocks light. The dark shape on the ground is the shadow.
White light is made of many colours. A rainbow shows them when sunlight goes through raindrops: red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet.

example.q: Why can you not see through a wooden door?
steps: Light travels in straight lines.
Wood blocks the light.
So no light passes through.

analogies.home: A hand in front of a torch makes a shadow on the wall.
analogies.nature: A tree makes a cool shadow in the heat.
analogies.city: A tall building makes a long shadow in the evening.

stages.mnemonic: Light goes straight; block it and you get a shadow.
terms: A dark shape made when light is blocked.
Colours made when sunlight passes through raindrops.
Lets light pass through, like clear glass.

misc.wrong: Shadows are things on their own.
misc.right: A shadow is just a place where light is blocked.

stages.limits: In this lesson, light is drawn as straight lines. Light also behaves in other ways that you will learn about later.

trip.prompt: Look for pictures of long and short shadows.

questions.q: What makes a shadow?
questions.why: A shadow forms where light is blocked.

questions.q: Which one gives light?
questions.why: The Sun makes light. The others do not.

questions.q: Light travels in...
questions.why: Light travels in straight lines in air.

questions.q: Which thing lets light pass through?
questions.why: Clear glass is transparent.

questions.q: Put the rainbow colours in order, starting with red.
questions.why: The rainbow goes red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet.

questions.q: Match each material.
questions.why: Different materials let different amounts of light pass.

questions.q: When is your shadow longest?
o: At noon when the Sun is high
questions.why: When the Sun is low in the sky, shadows are long.

questions.q: You want a shadow puppet show. What do you need?
o: Only a wall and a hat
questions.why: You need light and a screen to catch the shadow.

questions.q: Why is there no shadow in a completely dark room?
o: There is no light to block
The room is too cold for them
questions.why: A shadow is the absence of light, so you need light first.

questions.q: A rainbow appears when the Sun shines through rain. What does this show?
o: Sunlight has many colours in it
Rain has paint hidden in it
questions.why: Raindrops split white sunlight into its colours.

panel.q: Your shadow is short at noon. Where is the Sun?
panel.why: A high Sun makes short shadows.

panel.q: Why do we see a shadow behind a tree on a sunny day?
panel.model: The tree blocks the Sun's light, so a dark shadow forms behind it.
panel.why: A shadow forms where an object blocks light.

panel.q: What colour mixture is white sunlight?
panel.why: White light contains all colours.

teach.model: Light goes in straight lines. When something blocks the light, the place behind it is dark. That dark shape is a shadow. Shadows are long when the Sun is low and short when it is high.

points.ask: Where does light come from?
What does the object do to the light?
What do we see behind the object?

stages.title: Sound and vibrations
stages.hook: Touch your throat and hum. What do you feel?
explain: Sound is made when something shakes very fast. This shaking is called a vibration.
The shaking passes through air to your ears, and you hear it. Sound can also go through water and solid things.
A big, loud shake makes a loud sound. A fast shake makes a high sound, and a slow shake makes a low sound. There is no air in space, so sound cannot travel there.

example.q: A drum is hit and you hear it. What is moving?
steps: The drum skin shakes.
The air next to it shakes too.
The shaking reaches your ear.
example.a: The drum skin and the air shake.

analogies.music: A guitar string shakes and makes a note. Touch it and it stops.
analogies.home: A bell rings while it shakes. Hold it still and it goes quiet.
analogies.sea: A whale song travels through water.

stages.mnemonic: No shake, no sound; fast shake, high sound.
terms: What we hear when something shakes.
A very fast shaking back and forth.
How high or low a sound is.

misc.right: Sound needs something to travel through, like air, water or solids.

stages.limits: We use simple words here. Later you will learn how sound travels as a wave.

trip.prompt: Look for a picture of a drum or guitar and find the part that shakes.

questions.q: What makes sound?
questions.why: Sound comes from fast shaking.

questions.q: Which can make sound?
o: A calm lake with no wind
questions.why: A plucked string vibrates.

questions.q: How do you hear sound?
o: Light enters your ear and shakes it
questions.why: Vibrations travel through the air to your ear.

questions.q: A big drum hit hard makes a...
questions.why: A bigger shake makes a louder sound.

questions.q: A tiny whistle usually makes a...
questions.why: Small things shake fast and sound high.

questions.q: Put these sounds in order from lowest to highest.
questions.why: A tuba is low, a guitar is in the middle, a whistle is high.

questions.q: Match each to what vibrates.
questions.why: Each one shakes to make sound.

questions.q: You lightly touch a ringing bell and it goes quiet. Why?
questions.why: Stopping the shaking stops the sound.

questions.q: Why can you hear a friend's tap through a table when your ear is on it?
o: Sound only travels in air, never solids
questions.why: Sound travels through solids, often well.

questions.q: Why can astronauts not hear each other without radios in space?
o: There is no air to carry sound
Space is too bright to hear
questions.why: Sound needs something to travel through.

panel.q: A long ruler is held on a table and twanged. If you make the shaking part shorter, what happens to the sound?
panel.why: Shorter parts shake faster, so the sound is higher.

panel.q: How does sound get from a bell to your ear?
panel.model: The bell shakes, which shakes the air, and the shaking in the air reaches your ear.
panel.why: Sound travels as shaking through air to your ear.

panel.q: Sound reaches us after we see lightning. What does this tell us?
o: They go at the same speed
Lightning has no sound at all
panel.why: Light is much faster than sound, so we see lightning first.

teach.model: Sound comes from things that shake very fast. The shaking moves the air, and the moving air reaches your ear so you hear it. Bigger shakes sound louder. Faster shakes sound higher.

points.ask: What does something do to make sound?
How does it reach me?
What makes a sound loud or high?

stages.title: Hot, cold and temperature
stages.hook: Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a wooden spoon in the same room?
explain: Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is. We measure it with a thermometer, in degrees.
Heat moves from hot things to cold things. A cup of hot tea cools down because heat leaves it.
Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees Celsius. The Sun, a fire and a stove are sources of heat.

example.q: A hot soup sits on the table. What will happen to its temperature?
steps: Heat moves from hot to cold.
The room is cooler than the soup.
The soup gives heat to the air.

analogies.home: A hot bath slowly cools when you leave it.
analogies.nature: Snow melts when the Sun warms it.
analogies.farm: Milk is kept in a cool place so it stays fresh.

stages.mnemonic: Heat runs downhill, from hot to cold.
terms: How hot or cold something is.
Energy that moves from hot to cold.
To change from solid ice into water.

misc.right: Heat flows out of warm things. Cold is just less heat.

stages.limits: Feelings of hot and cold can fool us. Metal feels cold because it takes heat from your hand quickly.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of a thermometer and read what each line means.

questions.q: What tool measures temperature?
questions.why: A thermometer measures temperature.

questions.q: At what temperature in degrees Celsius does water freeze?
questions.why: Pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: At what temperature in degrees Celsius does water boil at sea level?
questions.why: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.

questions.q: Which is a source of heat?
questions.why: The Sun gives us heat.

questions.q: An ice cube sits in the sun. What happens?
questions.why: Heat from the Sun melts the ice.

questions.q: Which way does heat move?
questions.why: Heat always flows from hotter to colder things.

questions.q: Put these in order from coldest to hottest.
questions.why: Ice is coldest and boiling water is hottest.

questions.q: Match the item to what happens.
questions.why: Heat added melts or boils things; heat taken away freezes them.

questions.q: Hanna holds a cold drink in her warm hand. What happens to the drink?
questions.why: Heat moves from her warm hand into the drink.

questions.q: Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a wooden one?
o: Metal takes heat from your hand faster
Metal is colder than wood in the room
questions.why: They are the same temperature, but metal moves heat away from your hand faster.

panel.q: Why do we wear a coat in winter?
o: It slows heat leaving our body
It brings cold in from outside
panel.why: A coat keeps heat from escaping.

panel.q: Why does hot tea get cooler on a table?
panel.model: Heat moves from the hot tea into the cooler air, so the tea cools down.
panel.why: Heat flows from hot things to cold ones.

panel.q: A thermometer reads 5°C outside. Is that closer to freezing or boiling?
panel.why: 5°C is just above the freezing point of 0°C.

teach.model: Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is, and a thermometer measures it. Heat moves from hot things to colder things. That is why hot tea cools down and ice melts in the sun.

points.ask: What is temperature?
